Money can't buy happiness

— but community can

Institution
City St George's, University of London
Programme

Role

Duration
{{duration}} · {{year}}
Supervisor

Result
{{mark}}% · Distinction (MSc awarded with Merit)

Our relationships with family, neighbours, colleagues, friends and wider society are linked to how satisfied we are with life, but not in the same way everywhere. Using {{n_total}} survey responses from Austria, China, Russia, South Africa and the United States, I tested how culture, risk and the strength of the state change that link, and what that could mean for building better communities.

At a glance

  1. 01Social capital is positively associated with life satisfaction in all five countries, but the relationship is not uniform. Which forms of social capital matter depends on where you live.
  2. 02Both kinds of national context moderate the link: what governments shape (human development, government resources, corruption, income) and what a country is given (natural-disaster risk, cultural values).
  3. 03Most associations weaken as state capacity grows, but trust in fairness stays positive and significant in every country. Relative income has no significant main effect.

01

The question

We usually measure how well a country is doing by its income. But the relationships people have with family, neighbours, colleagues, friends and wider society are part of what makes life worth living, and they may not work the same way everywhere.

The quote on my desk

“Money can't buy happiness”: a maxim argued over since Rousseau's Discourse on the Arts and Sciences ({{rousseau}}). {{since_rousseau}} years later, the data still mostly agrees.

Does social capital make lives better everywhere, or does it depend on where you live? I tested it across five countries: Austria, China, Russia, South Africa and the United States.

Social capital research often treats its link with life satisfaction as uniform, and measures its dimensions with separate instruments.

My contribution was to use the underused ISSP {{issp}} module as a single instrument measuring all three of Putnam's social capital dimensions at once. National indices then served as moderators: what governments shape (human development, government resources, corruption and relative income) and what a country is given (natural-disaster risk and Hofstede's cultural values).

This gives a point of empirical comparison across national contexts, and it is the most portable part of the work.

02

Data & method

The data are the ISSP {{issp}} Social Networks module: {{n_total}} respondents in five countries, analysed in R. Life satisfaction is the module's single {{likert_max}}-point item. Social capital is measured through {{n_measures}} measures across five dimensions: trust, social networks, support resources, norms of reciprocity and contact.

Tool stack

R: mice, emmeans, car (VIF). Excel for early wrangling. The ISSP codebook as gospel.

Multi-item measures were reduced by PCA (most α ≥ {{alpha}}) after multiple imputation by MICE with predictive mean matching, grouped by country so each kept its own patterns. Country-level and pooled OLS with interaction terms tested four hypotheses; estimated marginal means and Tukey comparisons tested the differences between countries.

Quietly proud of

Reconstructing the ISCO-08 skill levels for Chinese agricultural workers, where the ISSP module has a known missing-data issue flagged on p. {{doc_page}} of its own documentation — so the Chinese sample didn't collapse.

Study specification

03

Findings

Social capital goes with higher satisfaction everywhere, and fairness most consistently

H1a· Within countries ·Supported

Within every country, almost all the significant links between social capital and life satisfaction were positive. Trust in fairness was positive and significant in all five (β {{fair_min}} to {{fair_max}}), and so was organisational trust (β {{ot_min}} to {{ot_max}}). Which other measures mattered varied from country to country (Fig. 1).

My reading

The surprise: organisational support resources went with lower life satisfaction, the opposite of what I expected. My reading is that people may dislike having to rely on institutions for what they need. It took me a week to see it.

My reading

Austria's fairness coefficient fits the idea of a ‘warm glow’ of trust in highly developed countries (Bjørnskov, 2003b): where systems are seen as fair, fairness itself may become part of a good life.

Same social capital, different lives: where you live still matters

H1b· Between countries ·Supported

Holding social capital at its sample mean, estimated life satisfaction still differed by country, from {{us_emm}} in the United States to {{cn_emm}} in China on the {{likert_min}}–{{likert_max}} scale. Every pair of countries differed significantly except two: {{tukey_note}}.

My reading

In China, guanxi (關係) networks are also how knowledge, licences, projects and careers flow. When social capital is an economic necessity rather than an extra, an average amount may not feel like enough. That may help explain China's lowest satisfaction at average social capital (He & Gebhardt, 2015).

My reading

Russia and South Africa leaned hardest on trust in society. Stable relationships may matter most when the wider situation feels uncertain.

What a country is given: risk and culture change which ties matter

H2a· Naturally occurring context ·Supported, with nuance

In riskier countries, trust and social networks were less strongly linked to satisfaction, and the societal care norm more strongly; risk itself had no significant association. Social networks mattered more in individualistic cultures, while societal care and organisational contact mattered more in collectivist ones. Power distance went with lower satisfaction, and masculinity with a stronger link for trust in fairness.

What governments shape: the more the state provides, the less social capital has to carry

H2b· Governed context ·Supported

Higher human development, more government resources and less corruption each went with higher satisfaction, and with weaker links between satisfaction and social networks, organisational support or organisational contact. Relative income had no significant main effect.

My reading

As income rose, trust and everyday contact mattered less for satisfaction, but the norm of caring for others in society mattered more. One explanation is that better-off people may draw wellbeing from pro-sociality rather than from income itself.

04

Limits

The design is cross-sectional, so association is the correct verb throughout. Any relationship here could reflect reverse causation (satisfied people invest more in community) or a third variable such as personality, which the ISSP doesn't measure.

R² around {{r2}} means the pooled model explains roughly a fifth of the variance in life satisfaction, within the normal range for this literature.

On income: household financial ease, a control for making ends meet, was one of the strongest predictors throughout (β {{fe_min}} to {{fe_max}}). Relative income did not predict satisfaction, but felt financial strain did.

Models were run within countries. Where the five are pooled to compare countries and test the national moderators, China contributes about {{cn_share}}% of the respondents ({{cn_n}} of {{n_total}}), so pooled estimates lean towards China and should be read with that in mind.

Life satisfaction is a single-item measure, and significance is read at p < .05 throughout this page.

The readings and the playbook that follow are interpretations of associations. They are ideas to test, not settled findings.

Overall, this is a very comprehensive study of the relationship between life satisfaction and social capital in various national contexts. It was a pleasure to read this thoughtful analysis.

Dr Anke Plagnol · supervisor
05

The playbook

Four low-cost ideas for building better communities, and how I'd test each one

Context first. Because the link between social capital and life satisfaction depends on culture and institutions, both need to be understood before any intervention is designed.

P1

Plan together before the flood

Where Countries with high natural-disaster risk

What the data show
In riskier countries, trust and social networks were less strongly linked to life satisfaction, while societal care was more strongly linked. Hazard risk itself had no positive association with satisfaction.
The idea
Community emergency action plans and regular community events. They build trust and organisational support, help protect people when disaster strikes, and cost little compared with large-scale infrastructure.
How I'd test it
Pilot plans in some at-risk neighbourhoods and compare with matched neighbourhoods. Measure trust, societal care and life satisfaction before, after, and again after the next hazard event.
P2

Pubs as policy

Where Individualistic cultures

What the data show
Social networks mattered more for life satisfaction in individualistic cultures, where there are fewer ready-made in-groups.
The idea
Subsidise or create ‘network drivers’ that build bridging ties between people who don't share an identity. These can be informal (parks, pubs) or formal (employment resource centres, national sporting events), alongside teaching tolerance and inclusivity from a young age.
How I'd test it
Stagger a community-space grant across areas. Measure bridging ties with a position generator (Lin) and life satisfaction over time, comparing early and late areas.
P3

Fairness is infrastructure

Where All contexts, especially advanced democracies

What the data show
Trust in fairness was positive and significant in every country, and Austria's coefficient was about twice the five-country average.
The idea
Treat perceived fairness as something to build: transparent institutions, justice even for petty crimes, fair wage distribution, and better social resource services. The dissertation also argues for progressive taxation.
How I'd test it
Follow perceived fairness and life satisfaction in a panel where a transparency or justice reform rolls out region by region.
P4

Community over cash

Where Developed societies

What the data show
Many social capital measures were positively associated with life satisfaction, while relative income had no significant main effect.
The idea
Development projects aimed at community resources and community trust may do more for wellbeing than economic promises. Treat barriers to social capital as a development challenge in their own right.
How I'd test it
Compare wellbeing outcomes of community-investment programmes with cost-matched cash or infrastructure programmes.

Theoretical implication. Significant interactions suggest limits to what institutions alone can do for wellbeing, because culture and physical environment shape how citizens interact.

06

What I'd do next

This is a small step in a large literature.

A wider sample. Five countries is diverse but not globally representative. A wider sample would test generalisability and give a measured point of comparison for adapting development ideas across cultures.

Personality. Personal characteristics and personality traits may mediate or moderate the relationship; a dedicated dataset could test this. Tulin, Lancee and Volker (2018) show personality traits predict forms of social capital, and the ISSP doesn't measure them.

Better norms. Norms need better proxies. A dedicated questionnaire polling a truly worldwide sample would help.

The design. A longitudinal panel, even two waves, would separate “social capital comes first” from “satisfied people build social capital”.

Future research. The multidimensional nature of social capital, its long-term consequences, which promotion strategies work, and the critical circumstances where it matters most.

These simple relationships: with family, neighbours, colleagues, friends, and broader society have the power to make life worth living.
